chapitres.resume:
## Le cours (contrat didactique 2026-2027)

- **60 heures/an**, 2 h par semaine ; plusieurs professeurs selon les groupes.
- ==Pas un cours pour débutants : niveau **B1** fortement conseillé au départ ; objectif **B2 (upper-intermediate)**.== Le **test de positionnement** est obligatoire (première semaine), sinon pas d'accès aux dispositifs d'accompagnement.
- **Préparations à domicile indispensables et obligatoires** ; présence active ; **pas d'ordinateur, tablette ni smartphone** en classe.
- Objectifs : lexique et grammaire B2, compréhension orale et écrite, expression orale sur les médias et la société, argumentation écrite.
- Supports sur **Learn** (seule source fiable) ; *Murphy's English Grammar in Use* (4e ou 5e éd.) à se procurer ; syllabus *UE1 English Vocabulary*.

## Évaluation (60 points)

| Quand | Épreuve | Points |
|---|---|---|
| Semaines 11-12 | **Oral : Round Table Discussion** | 15 |
| Semaine 13 | **Écrit : vocabulaire Q1 + grammaire du 1er semestre** | 10 |
| 2e semestre | Oral : présentations (**Press Review**) | 15 |
| Semaine 26 | Écrit : vocabulaire Q2 + grammaire de l'année + contenu Q2 | 20 |

- Il faut avoir **participé à toutes les évaluations**. Seconde session : toute la matière de l'année, toutes les épreuves ; **aucun report de note** entre sessions.
- Absence : envoyer le justificatif **au professeur** au plus vite, sous peine d'ajournement.
- Critères : **intelligibilité** et **respect des consignes** ; pertinence, cohérence, rigueur et richesse grammaticales et lexicales ; à l'oral, **fluidité** et attitude communicationnelle verbale et non verbale.

## Planning d'autoformation (semestre 1) — matière d'examen

| Semaine | En classe | Vocabulaire | Grammaire (Murphy) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1-2 (15-25 sept.) | Introduction, Topic 1 | — | — |
| 3 | Topic 1 | Units 1-3 | Units 1-6 |
| 4 | Topic 1 | Units 4-5 | Units 7-12 |
| 5 | Topic 1 | Units 6-7 | Units 13-18 |
| 6 | Topic 2 | Units 8-10 | Units 19-25 |
| 7 | Topic 2 | Units 11-13 | Units 69-72 |
| 8 | Topic 2 | Units 14-15 | Units 73-79 |
| 9 | Topic 2 | Units 16-18 | Units 80-81 + 85-88 |
| 10 | Révision, entraînement round table | — | Revision 113, 115, 119, 120 |
| 11-12 | Oral : round table | | |
| 13 | Test écrit | | |

*Seules les unités de grammaire 1 à 6 sont dans le dossier Drive : étudie les autres dans ton Murphy.*

## L'oral : Round Table Discussion

- Groupes de **3 ou 4** ; un énoncé ou une question liée à un des **thèmes du semestre** (AI-generated art, the loneliness economy).
- **20 minutes de préparation individuelle**, puis **20 minutes de discussion**.
- Le but n'est pas de « gagner » mais de **contribuer** : construire une **informed opinion**, comprendre plusieurs perspectives (*Critics argue that… / Supporters highlight that…*), prendre une position claire et nuancée (*However, I personally think that…*), réagir aux autres.
- ==**Informed opinion** : montrer qu'on connaît les principaux arguments (articles, vidéos, cours), les reformuler, puis ajouter sa perspective avec exemples ou raisonnement.== « AI is cool, I like it » → pas informé.
- S'inscrire sur la liste publiée par le professeur avant la date limite, sinon pas d'accès au test.

## Speaking Guide : développer une discussion

1. **Introduire le sujet général** ;
2. **Expliquer les enjeux** (pourquoi c'est pertinent ou controversé) ;
3. **Définir les termes clés** ;
4. **Donner des exemples concrets** (matière du cours, statistiques, expériences) — points 1-4 = **contextualisation** ;
5. **Présenter différents points de vue** (pour/contre) ;
6. **Se poser des questions** (*Can you explain what you mean by that? / Do you have an example?*) ;
7. **Réagir aux autres** (*I see your point, but I think…*) ;
8. **Nuancer** (pas de noir et blanc) ;
9. **Conclure ensemble** (résumer, accords et désaccords).

**Expressions utiles** : demander un avis (*Do you think we should…? Would you rather…? What do you think of…? Wouldn't you agree that…?*) ; présenter des arguments (*The main thing is… / First of all… / Moreover…*) ; donner son opinion (*In my view… / I strongly believe… / If you ask me…*) ; certitude (*Clearly… / There's no doubt that…*) ; accord (*Exactly! / I couldn't agree with you more*) ; accord partiel (*I agree up to a point, however… / You have a point there, but…*).

chapitres.resume:
## Key concepts to define

The course notes ask you to define, in one sentence each:

- **Core**: artificial intelligence, **generative AI**, AI art, **creativity**;
- **Technology**: **machine learning**, **algorithm**, **training data**;
- **Art**: artist, **authorship**, **originality**;
- **Ethics and law**: **copyright**, **intellectual property**, ethical issues;
- **Economy**: **automation**, **creative industries**.

Core question: **"What is art?"** (quotes by Merton, Seneca, Tanning, Emerson, Nietzsche…). Works compared in class: Glenn Brown (*In my time of dying*), Refik Anadol (*ISS Dreams*)…

**Useful vocabulary**: *prompt, creative medium, groundbreaking, to revolutionize, artistic style, AI enthusiast* (opportunities) vs *copyright, compensation* (debates).

## Reading: Eric Reinhart — "The trouble with AI art isn't just lack of originality"

Eric Reinhart is a political anthropologist and social psychiatrist. His thesis: ==when artwork is invented by a machine, it **loses its most important power: to help people connect**.==

- Art's value lies not in the object but in what it carries: traces of the artist's **interiority**, an act of **transmission**; the viewer finds in it a reflection of their own fears and desires.
- Art also connects **audiences with each other** (watching films with lovers, painting murals with neighbours).
- This connectedness underpins a **democratic ethos**: we share fundamental aspects of being *because of* our differences. Without it, ties **fray** and are replaced by tribalism, authoritarianism, exclusion.
- The machine does not desire, has no body, no interiority: AI work is "**uninhabited**".

Vocabulary: *alienation, connection, vulnerability, community, thingification, empathy, isolation, exploitation; ineffable, interiority, to commune, to foster, endeavor, simulacrum, to probe, ubiquitous, to diminish, to nurture, to erode*.

## Four perspectives

| Perspective | Idea |
|---|---|
| **1. AI as a positive tool** | a new creative medium (like photography once), new possibilities, more accessible art |
| **2. AI threatens human artists** | automation of creative jobs, works used without consent, reduced value of human skills |
| **3. AI cannot truly create art** | no emotions, no lived experience, no interiority (Reinhart) |
| **4. AI challenges traditional definitions of art** | questions about authorship, originality and what counts as art |

**Causes → consequences** (class exercise): AI trained on artworks → debate about copyright / authorship; more people use AI tools → new artistic possibilities; artists fear automation → employment concerns; AI creates images in seconds → faster creative processes; companies collect large datasets → ethical concerns.

## Round-table questions to prepare

1. Is art generated by AI really art?
2. Can AI revolutionize the art world by enabling new forms of creativity?
3. Should AI works be exhibited in museums alongside traditional art?
4. If AI is trained on artworks without consent, is AI art plagiarism?
5. Does art require human emotions?
6. Should artists be compensated when their work trains AI models?
7. Is prompting an AI a form of artistic skill?
8. Should museums support human artists over AI works?
9. Can AI democratize art?
10. Are the risks of AI art greater than its benefits?

> Model sentence: *Critics argue that AI art threatens artists' jobs. Supporters highlight that it makes creation more accessible. However, I personally think that…*
pointsCles: Define the key concepts: generative AI, training data, authorship, originality, copyright, automation, creative industries.
Reinhart: AI art loses art's main power, helping people connect; machine-made work is "uninhabited".
Art connects artist and viewer, and viewers with each other; this underpins democracy.
Four perspectives: positive tool, threat to artists, not true art, challenge to definitions of art.
Prepare arguments and counterarguments for the ten round-table questions.

definitions.def: AI that produces new content (images, text, music) from prompts, after being trained on existing data.
The large set of existing works or data used to train an AI model.
The question of who is the author of a work (here: the user, the AI, the company?).
The legal right of an author over the use and reproduction of their work.
The instruction given to a generative AI to produce a result.
An artist's inner life and feelings, which, for Reinhart, an AI work does not carry.
An imitation or copy that lacks the substance of the original; how some critics describe AI art.

fiches.q: What is Eric Reinhart's main thesis about AI art?
fiches.r: When art is made by a machine, it loses its most important power: helping people connect.

fiches.q: According to Reinhart, where does art's value lie?
fiches.r: Not in the object but in what it transmits: traces of the artist's interiority, which viewers connect to.

fiches.q: Why does Reinhart link art to democracy?
fiches.r: Shared aesthetic experience affirms our differences while connecting us; without it, social ties fray and are replaced by tribalism and authoritarianism.

fiches.q: Why does Reinhart call AI work "uninhabited"?
fiches.r: The machine does not desire, has no body and no interiority: there is no self behind the work.

fiches.q: What are the four perspectives on AI art studied in class?
fiches.r: AI as a positive tool; AI threatens human artists; AI cannot truly create art; AI challenges traditional definitions of art.

fiches.q: Give two arguments for AI as an opportunity.
fiches.r: It opens new creative possibilities (a new medium, like photography) and makes artistic creation more accessible.

fiches.q: Give two arguments for AI as a threat.
fiches.r: It may replace creative jobs and exploit existing artworks used as training data without consent.

fiches.q: Which legal and ethical concepts are central to the AI-art debate?
fiches.r: Copyright, intellectual property, authorship, consent and compensation of artists.

fiches.q: What is the consequence of AI being trained on artworks?
Complete the word family: create / ___ / creative.
fiches.r: creation (also: connect – connection, imagine – imagination, innovate – innovation, express – expression, participate – participation).

quiz.q: For Reinhart, the biggest problem with AI art is:
choix: the loss of art's power to connect people
quiz.explication: The title says it's "something far bigger" than originality.

quiz.q: "AI is simply another artistic tool" represents:
quiz.explication: Perspective 1.

quiz.q: "AI lacks emotions and lived experience" supports the view that:
quiz.explication: Perspective 3.

quiz.q: Which word has a negative connotation?
quiz.explication: Like isolation, exploitation, thingification.

## Warm-up

Would you pay for it? A therapist, a dating app, a coworking space, a solo-dining restaurant, a solo travel group, someone to have dinner with you, a fake friend at an event, an **AI companion**, an **AI romantic partner**, a **robot companion** for an elderly person… All these services belong to the **loneliness economy**. Film discussed: ***Her*** (2013) — Theodore falls for an AI, Samantha ("You always wanted to have a wife without the challenges of actually dealing with anything real").

## Reading: "Welcome to the Loneliness Economy" (Sam Goldstein, *Psychology Today*, October 2025)

==In an age of digital overload, **loneliness has become profitable**: companionship can now be bought, streamed or rented.==

| Place | What happened | What it tells us |
|---|---|---|
| **Japan (2025)** | approval of **robot companions** for an ageing population; *kodokushi* ("lonely deaths") | a technological answer to a human crisis |
| **United Kingdom (2018)** | **Tracey Crouch**, world's first **Minister for Loneliness** | isolation recognized as a public issue |
| **United States (2023)** | the Surgeon General's report calls loneliness an "**epidemic**", as harmful as smoking **15 cigarettes a day**; many Gen Zers' closest confidants are apps | a public-health crisis |
| **Seoul / Tokyo** | **solo dining booths**; renting an *ossan* (older man) to talk or walk | new services built on isolation |
| **Online** | **Replika** (AI chatbot "soulmate"), therapy apps, wellness retreats, pet rentals | a market feeding an emotional hunger |

**Four reasons** for the loneliness economy: traditional places of community (churches, neighbourhood centres, offices) have **faded**; **remote work** keeps people apart; a culture that **glorifies independence** makes asking for company feel like weakness; above all, **technology** — Sherry Turkle's "**alone together**": surrounded by screens yet starving for something real; **outsourced intimacy** with influencers and fictional characters.

**A global shift**: in **collectivist** cultures isolation carries shame; in **individualistic** ones it's brushed off as "just being an adult".

**Hope or harm?** ==A **lifeline** for people with anxiety, disabilities or in rural areas, and it normalizes seeking support — but many systems are designed for **engagement, not healing**== ("they keep us clicking, but not connecting"). Julianne Holt-Lunstad: chronic loneliness → heart disease, depression.

**Reimagining togetherness**: the loneliness economy is a **mirror** of our disconnection. Solution: more **public spaces** where people meet ("parks instead of parking lots, town halls instead of timelines") — "it'll take us showing up for each other".

**Vocabulary from the text**: *prevalence, utterly, void, to capitalize on, to stroll, weary, craving, untethered, to outsource, surrogate, to brush off, to ache, curated, to splinter*.
pointsCles: The loneliness economy: companionship that can be bought, streamed or rented (AI companions, solo dining, rented friends).
Key facts: Japan's robot companions (2025), UK Minister for Loneliness (2018), US Surgeon General's "epidemic" (2023, = 15 cigarettes a day).
Causes: decline of community places, remote work, culture of independence, technology ("alone together").
Hope: a lifeline for some; harm: designed for engagement, not healing.
Solution proposed: real public spaces and people showing up for each other.

definitions.def: The market of products and services sold to people who feel lonely (AI companions, solo dining, rented company…).
Japanese term for "lonely deaths": people dying alone and unnoticed.
Sherry Turkle's phrase: constantly connected through screens, yet lacking real connection.
Having nothing solid to hold on to; disconnected.
A replacement or substitute (here: digital substitutes for human relationships).
The time and attention users spend on an app, which many services are designed to maximize.

fiches.r: A market where companionship, digital or otherwise, can be bought, streamed or rented.

fiches.q: Who was the world's first Minister for Loneliness, and when?
fiches.r: Tracey Crouch, in the United Kingdom, in 2018.

fiches.q: How did the US Surgeon General describe loneliness in 2023?
fiches.r: As an "epidemic", with health risks comparable to smoking 15 cigarettes a day.

fiches.q: What did Japan approve in 2025, and why?
fiches.r: Robot companions for its ageing population, in response to kodokushi ("lonely deaths").

fiches.q: Give three examples of loneliness-economy services.
fiches.r: Replika (AI chatbot), solo dining booths in Seoul and Tokyo, renting an ossan to talk or walk (also therapy apps, pet rentals).

fiches.q: What are the four reasons for the rise of the loneliness economy?
fiches.r: The decline of community places, remote work, a culture glorifying independence, and technology ("alone together").

fiches.q: What does Sherry Turkle mean by "alone together"?
fiches.r: We are always surrounded by screens and messages, yet starving for real connection.

fiches.q: For whom can these services be a "lifeline"?
fiches.r: People with anxiety, disabilities, or those living in rural areas.

fiches.q: What is the main criticism of these services?
fiches.r: They are designed for engagement, not healing: they keep us clicking, not connecting.
More public spaces where people actually meet (parks, town halls) and people showing up for each other.

fiches.q: What is the difference between constant interaction and genuine connection?
fiches.r: Interaction is frequent digital contact; genuine connection involves empathy, touch and shared experience with real people.

quiz.q: Which country appointed the first Minister for Loneliness?
quiz.explication: Tracey Crouch, 2018.
A Japanese term.
Some users call it their "soulmate".
MIT sociologist, 2011.

chapitres.resume:
*Résumé des unités 1 à 6 de Murphy, English Grammar in Use (les autres unités au programme sont dans ton livre).*

## Unit 1 — Present continuous (I am doing)

**am/is/are + -ing**. Utilisations :

- une action **en cours au moment où l'on parle**, pas terminée (*I'm trying to work. It isn't raining any more.*) ;
- une action **commencée et pas finie**, même si on ne la fait pas à l'instant (*I'm reading a really good book. Kate is learning Italian.*) ;
- avec **today / this week / this year** (périodes autour de maintenant) ;
- un **changement en cours** (*getting, becoming, changing, improving, increasing, rising…* : *The population of the world is increasing very fast.*).

## Unit 2 — Present simple (I do)

- **Vérités générales**, actions **répétées** (*The earth goes round the sun. The cafe opens at 7.30.*) ; **fréquence** (*How often do you…?*).
- 3e personne : **-s / -es** (*he works, she teaches, he has*).
- Questions et négations avec **do/does** : *What does this word mean?* (pas *What means…*) ; *Rice doesn't grow in cold climates.*
- **Verbes performatifs** : *I promise / I apologise / I advise / I insist / I agree / I refuse / I suggest* (pas *I'm promising*).

## Unit 3 — Present continuous vs present simple (1)

| Continuous | Simple |
|---|---|
| en cours, autour de maintenant (*The water is boiling.*) | général, répété (*Water boils at 100 °C.*) |
| **temporaire** (*I'm living with friends until I find a place.*) | **permanent** (*My parents live in London.*) |

==**I always do** = à chaque fois ; **I'm always doing** = trop souvent, avec agacement== (*I'm always losing my keys. He's always complaining.*).

## Unit 4 — Present continuous vs present simple (2)

- **Verbes d'état** normalement **pas au continu** : *like, want, need, prefer, know, realise, understand, recognise, believe, suppose, remember, mean, belong, fit, contain, consist, seem* (*I want something to eat*, pas *I'm wanting*).
- **think** : = *croire, avoir une opinion* → simple (*I think Mary is Canadian*) ; = *considérer, réfléchir* → continu possible (*I'm thinking of giving up my job*).
- **see, hear, smell, taste** → normalement **simple** (*Do you see that man? This soup doesn't taste good.*) ; **look / feel** (état actuel) → simple ou continu (*You look well / You're looking well*), mais *I usually feel tired* (simple).
- **am/is/are being** + adjectif = **comportement** actuel contrôlable (*He's being so selfish* — d'habitude il ne l'est pas) ; impossible pour *ill, tired*.

## Unit 5 — Past simple (I did)

- Réguliers en **-ed** (*worked, stopped, studied*) ; nombreux **irréguliers** (*write → wrote, see → saw, go → went, shut → shut*).
- Questions et négations : **did/didn't + infinitif** (*Did you enjoy it? I didn't buy anything.*) ; *What did you do?* (pas *What did you?*).
- **be** → *was/were* (*I wasn't hungry. Were you too tired?*).

## Unit 6 — Past continuous (I was doing)

- **was/were + -ing** : être **au milieu** d'une action à un moment passé (*At 10.30 they were playing tennis.*).
- ==Action longue (continu) **interrompue** par une action courte (simple)== : *Matt phoned while we were having dinner. It was raining when I got up.*
- Actions **successives** → past simple : *When Karen arrived, we had dinner* (elle arrive, puis on mange) ≠ *we were having dinner* (déjà commencé).
- Les **verbes d'état** restent au simple (*We knew each other well*, pas *were knowing*).
pointsCles: Present continuous (am/is/are + -ing) : action en cours, temporaire, changement en cours.
Present simple : vérités générales, habitudes, fréquence ; do/does pour questions et négations.
I'm always doing = trop souvent (agacement) ; I always do = à chaque fois.
Les verbes d'état (know, want, like, believe, belong, seem…) ne se mettent pas au continu.
think : opinion → simple ; réflexion → continu possible.
Past simple : -ed ou irrégulier ; did/didn't + infinitif.
Past continuous : action en cours dans le passé, souvent interrompue par un past simple.

definitions.def: am/is/are + -ing : action en cours ou temporaire autour du moment présent.
Forme de base (+ -s à la 3e personne) : vérités générales, habitudes, situations permanentes.
Verbes non utilisés au continu : like, want, need, know, understand, believe, belong, seem…
Verbe en -ed ou forme irrégulière : action terminée dans le passé.
was/were + -ing : action en cours à un moment du passé.

fiches.q: Peut-on dire « I'm reading a book » si on ne lit pas à l'instant ?
fiches.r: Oui : on a commencé le livre et on ne l'a pas fini (action en cours au sens large).

fiches.q: Quel temps pour un changement en cours (population, niveau d'anglais) ?
fiches.r: Le present continuous : The population is increasing. Is your English getting better?

fiches.q: Pourquoi dit-on « I promise I won't be late » et pas « I'm promising » ?
fiches.r: Avec les verbes performatifs (promise, apologise, suggest, insist, agree, refuse…), on utilise le present simple.

fiches.q: Différence entre « I'm living with friends » et « My parents live in London » ?
fiches.r: Continu = situation temporaire ; simple = situation permanente.
Il se plaint trop souvent (always + continu = agacement).

fiches.q: Cite six verbes d'état qu'on ne met pas au continu.
fiches.r: like, want, need, know, understand, believe (aussi remember, mean, belong, fit, contain, consist, seem…).
I think = opinion (I think Mary is Canadian) ; I'm thinking = réflexion (I'm thinking of selling my car).
Pour un comportement actuel et contrôlable (He's being so selfish today) ; pas pour ill ou tired.

fiches.q: Comment forme-t-on les questions et négations au past simple ?
fiches.r: did/didn't + infinitif : Did you enjoy it? I didn't buy anything.

fiches.q: Donne le past simple de write, see, go, shut.
Comment forme-t-on le past continuous et quand l'utilise-t-on ?
fiches.r: was/were + -ing : action en cours à un moment passé (At 10.30 they were playing tennis).

fiches.q: Différence : « When Karen arrived, we had dinner » / « we were having dinner » ?
fiches.r: had = on a mangé après son arrivée ; were having = on avait déjà commencé quand elle est arrivée.

fiches.q: Complète : Matt phoned while we ___ (have) dinner.
fiches.r: were having (action longue au continu, interrompue par le past simple).

quiz.explication: Vérité générale → present simple.

quiz.q: Please be quiet. I ___ to work.
quiz.explication: Action en cours → present continuous.
want est un verbe d'état.

quiz.q: I ___ my keys again! I'm always losing them.
quiz.explication: Exemple de Murphy : I've lost my keys again. I'm always losing them.
Action en cours (continu) quand une autre se produit (simple).
do est ici le verbe principal.
taste (sens) → present simple.
